sources.title: Guidelines for Personal Hygiene During an Emergency
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
sources.supports: Handwashing with soap and water for at least 20 seconds; boiled or disinfected water for handwashing only if local authorities or a doctor recommend extra caution; a temporary handwashing station from a large water jug; alcohol-based sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol and its limits (does not eliminate all germs, may not remove chemicals, less effective on visibly dirty or greasy hands); bathing guidance and when not to bathe (sewage, toxic chemicals, flood-contaminated rivers, streams and lakes); brushing teeth with clean water; protecting wounds (Vibrio, waterproof bandage, seek care for redness, swelling or oozing); pointer to CDC diapering fact sheets.
sources.notes: Page shows 'Updated: July 18, 2024' before 'Published: September 16, 2024'; both recorded as shown. Upgrades the register placeholder of the same id.

sources.title: NOAA Weather Radio (NWS Cheyenne office page)
sources.publisher: National Weather Service, Cheyenne, WY Weather Forecast Office
sources.supports: NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards is a nationwide network broadcasting official warnings, watches, forecasts and other hazard information 24 hours a day; it works with the FCC's Emergency Alert System; a special radio is needed; useful receiver features are Tone Alert, Specific Area Message Encoding (SAME) to alert for your county only, and battery backup.
sources.notes: A regional (Cheyenne) office page, kept because it is the URL listed in the register placeholder. It carries no publication or review date. The national page (health-nws-nwr-national) is the one cited for frequencies and coverage. Upgrades the register placeholder of the same id.

sources.title: NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards (national program page)
sources.supports: NWR is a nationwide network of radio stations broadcasting from the nearest NWS office; it also carries warnings for non-weather hazards (earthquakes, chemical releases, AMBER alerts, 911 telephone outages); more than 1,000 transmitters covering all 50 states, coastal waters, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands and U.S. Pacific territories; a special receiver or scanner is required; seven VHF frequencies (162.400 to 162.550 MHz); the page lists transmitters that are degraded or out of service and says to check county coverage listings for alternate transmitters.
sources.notes: Undated page. It displays a live list of transmitter outages, so its content changes continuously. Read scope: full page as returned, including the live outage list; the linked FAQ, alert-information and receiver pages were not opened.

sources.title: What to Do to Protect Yourself During a Power Outage
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
sources.supports: Medication safety in an outage: some drugs need refrigeration to keep their strength; when the power is out for a day or more, throw away refrigerated medication unless the label says otherwise; if a life depends on a refrigerated drug that has been at room temperature, use it only until a new supply is available; replace refrigerated drugs as soon as possible. Also: safe water for drinking, cooking and hygiene is bottled, boiled or treated; carbon monoxide rules (never run a generator indoors or less than 20 feet from a window, door or vent; Poison Control 1-800-222-1222); fridge and freezer hold times.
sources.notes: Page shows 'Updated: January 26, 2024' while also showing 'Reviewed: August 26, 2026'; both recorded as shown.

sources.title: Guidelines for Septic and Onsite Wastewater Systems
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
sources.supports: Emergencies can damage sewer systems and cause untreated wastewater to overflow; avoid contact with floodwater that may contain sewage; signs a septic system is not working; limit toilet flushing, dishwashing, laundry and showering during an emergency; flush toilets as little as possible or use a temporary toilet; do not pump a septic tank more than halfway after flooding; do not drink well water until it is known to be safe; have a damaged system professionally inspected.
sources.notes: Written for flood and similar emergencies.

sources.title: Potential Sanitation Solutions During an Emergency Response (archived)
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (archive.cdc.gov; NCEZID, Division of Foodborne, Waterborne, and Environmental Diseases)
sources.supports: In emergencies, preventing open defecation and containing waste are critical to reducing disease spread; handwashing facilities with soap and water belong at every sanitation facility; a comparison of packet latrines, bucket latrines, chemical toilets, trench and pit latrines and ecological-sanitation toilets with their advantages and constraints (flooding, high water table, access for disabled, elderly and small children, disposal needs).
sources.notes: ARCHIVED CDC page, not maintained, written for emergency response in settlements and cholera-prone areas (global WASH), not for a single household. Cited only for general principles and the options comparison, never for household quantities.

sources.title: Safe Drug Use After a Natural Disaster
sources.publisher: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (Center for Drug Evaluation and Research)
sources.supports: Keep a current medicine list (name, strength, purpose, amount and timing, conditions, supplies, allergies) and a copy of prescriptions; know how much you have; get early refills if pharmacy access may be disrupted; ask a pharmacist or provider about an emergency supply and state emergency refill laws; watertight containers kept above flood risk; a plan to keep refrigerated medicines cold with a cooler and ice or gel packs; discard medicines that touched floodwater or unsafe water; consider replacing medicines exposed to fire heat; limited exception for lifesaving drugs; reconstitute only with purified or bottled water; for refrigerated medicines check the storage instructions or ask a pharmacist, provider or manufacturer; life-sustaining medicine may be used until a replacement is available.
sources.notes: Date taken from the page's modified-time metadata (09/01/2026); the page body shows no visible date.

sources.title: Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an Emergency
sources.publisher: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (Center for Drug Evaluation and Research)
sources.supports: Label storage for insulin in a refrigerator at about 36 F to 46 F; manufacturer vials or cartridges, opened or unopened, can be left at 59 F to 86 F for up to 28 days; diluted or decanted insulin discarded within two weeks; extreme temperatures reduce effectiveness; do not use frozen insulin; keep insulin away from heat and sun; insulin in a pump's infusion set discarded after 48 hours unless the pump's instructions differ; call the manufacturer with questions; and the page's own instruction that insulin should be switched under a doctor's care with close blood-sugar monitoring.
sources.notes: The page also contains unit-conversion tables for switching between insulin products. This archive deliberately does NOT reproduce them. Date taken from page metadata (modified 09/28/2026). The page's manufacturer phone table is not reproduced either, because the page itself says the numbers change. Read scope: full page as returned, including the switching tables (not reproduced).

sources.title: FDA Offers Tips about Medical Devices and Natural Disasters
sources.publisher: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (Center for Devices and Radiological Health)
sources.supports: Keep devices and supplies clean and dry; people who depend on a device to stay alive should seek emergency services and, if possible, ask the local public health authority about evacuation before adverse weather; tell the electric company and fire department about a device that needs power; ask the manufacturer or distributor whether a device can run on batteries or a generator; do not plug in a wet cord or device; devices often reset to a default mode when power is interrupted, so check settings when power returns; do not reuse single-use devices; clean multi-use devices only as the manufacturer directs and do not boil them unless the label allows; heat and humidity can affect glucose meters and test strips; use dry ice or instant cold packs rather than ice if water contamination is a danger; devices such as dialyzers and IV pumps need safe water; carbon monoxide warning for generators.
sources.notes: SOURCE DISAGREEMENT: this page gives its own bleach-dosing figures (for 5.25% bleach, 1/8 teaspoon per gallon of clear water, 1/4 teaspoon if cloudy) that differ from the CDC table in making-water-safer (8 drops per gallon, double if cloudy). The medical-devices guide does NOT reprint either; it points to the water guide and to the device manufacturer. Reviewer to note the discrepancy for the lead.

sources.title: About the HHS emPOWER Program
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (ASPR, with CMS)
sources.supports: emPOWER, launched in 2013 by ASPR and CMS, uses Medicare claims data to give public health authorities, emergency managers and responders de-identified counts of at-risk people who rely on electricity-dependent durable medical equipment and certain essential health services (dialysis, home oxygen, home health, hospice); its data covers over 4.6 million Medicare beneficiaries; prolonged outages can put such individuals in life-threatening situations within hours or days; it is a program for partners, and the page does not tell individuals how to enrol or what to do themselves.
sources.notes: The program home page and About page address public health authorities, not individual households. We found no individual self-registration instructions on either page, and do not claim there are none elsewhere.

sources.title: Power Outages
sources.supports: A power outage may prevent use of medical devices; have alternate plans for refrigerating medicines or powering medical devices; inventory the items that rely on electricity and plan for batteries, power banks and other alternatives; talk to your medical provider about an outage plan for powered devices and refrigerated medicines, ask how long a medication can be stored at higher temperatures, and get specific guidance for life-critical medications; if power is out for more than a day, discard refrigerated medication unless the label says otherwise and consult a doctor or pharmacist for a new supply; generator and carbon monoxide rules (outdoors, at least 20 feet from windows, doors and attached garages).
sources.notes: Read scope: full page as returned; linked PDFs not opened except the December 2023 fact sheet, which is registered separately (health-fema-power-outage-sheet).

sources.title: People with Disabilities
sources.supports: Support network; many city and county emergency management agencies keep voluntary registries for people with disabilities; know more than one dialysis or treatment facility; ask the power provider for priority power restoration; organize prescriptions; medical alert tags; list of device styles and serial numbers; backup oxygen; spare batteries and a manual backup for a power wheelchair; keep model information and where equipment came from; weather radio with text display and flashing alert for people who are deaf or hard of hearing; extra hearing-aid batteries; FEMA App alerts for up to five locations; several days' supply of prescription medicines.
sources.notes: Read scope: full page as returned; linked PDFs and videos were not opened.

sources.title: Build A Kit
sources.supports: Basic kit items include water (one gallon per person per day for several days, for drinking and sanitation), a battery-powered or hand-crank radio and a NOAA Weather Radio with tone alert, flashlight, extra batteries, whistle, moist towelettes, garbage bags and plastic ties for personal sanitation, local maps, and a cell phone with chargers and a backup battery; additional items include soap, hand sanitizer, prescription medications, feminine supplies, diapers and wipes, and personal hygiene items.
sources.notes: Read scope: full page as returned; the linked printable checklist PDF was not opened.

sources.title: Make A Plan
sources.supports: Plan around five questions, the first being how you will receive emergency alerts and warnings; know how you will contact one another and reconnect if separated; pick a familiar, easy-to-find family meeting place; account for medical needs including prescriptions and equipment, disabilities and access needs, languages, pets and service animals; document and practice the plan.
sources.notes: Read scope: full page as returned; the fillable plan form and linked PDFs were not opened.

sources.title: Emergency Alerts
sources.supports: Wireless Emergency Alerts (short alerts to WEA-enabled phones in a locally targeted area; unique sound and vibration; not affected by network congestion; no charge, no subscription; older phones may not be capable and some phones require WEA to be enabled; some carriers call them Government Alerts or Emergency Alert Messages); the Emergency Alert System (broadcast TV and radio, satellite audio, cable); NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards; IPAWS (FEMA does not review, edit or approve alerts); the FEMA App (NWS alerts for up to five locations, shelter finder).
sources.notes: Read scope: full page as returned; linked PDFs (WEA fact sheet, guide for alerts and warnings) were not opened.

sources.title: Integrated Public Alert & Warning System
sources.supports: IPAWS is FEMA's national system for local alerting; alerts are authenticated and delivered through multiple pathways at once (Emergency Alert System via AM, FM and satellite radio and broadcast, cable and satellite TV; Wireless Emergency Alerts to phones by location, 'even if cellular networks are overloaded'; NOAA Weather Radio; internet services; sirens and digital road signs); more than 2,000 federal, state, local, tribal and territorial alerting authorities use it; multiple pathways increase the likelihood a message reaches the public.
sources.notes: Read scope: full page as returned; linked fact sheets, myths-and-facts and FAQ pages were not opened.

sources.title: Wireless Emergency Alerts
sources.supports: WEA delivers warnings to wireless devices; wireless provider participation is voluntary but participating providers must meet FCC requirements; alerts are sent by authorized officials through IPAWS to providers and pushed from cell towers to devices in the affected area; WEA and the Emergency Alert System are the two main components of the national public warning system; the page lists a 2023 FCC item seeking partners to test delivering alerts during cell tower outages (the item itself was not read).
sources.notes: The FCC page's own robots metadata is 'noindex'; the content is nonetheless live on fcc.gov. Read scope: the explanatory text and resources list; the long releases archive (2007-2026 rulemaking and waiver titles) was scanned for titles only, and no archive item was opened.

sources.title: Tips for Communicating in an Emergency
sources.supports: Emergencies create network congestion; limit non-emergency calls and keep calls brief; try text messaging, which may go through when a call will not; try several services (text, email, landline); wait 10 seconds before redialing; have charged batteries and car-charger adapters; keep emergency numbers in the phone; place calls while the vehicle is stationary; have a family communications plan with an out-of-area central contact; forward a home number to a wireless number when evacuating; keep a corded phone that does not depend on electricity; for people with disabilities, medical alert systems usually need a working phone line so keep a backup.
sources.notes: Undated; some wording (pagers, PDAs, text radio) reflects older technology. Cited for its congestion advice, which it states generally.

sources.title: Toilet Use During an Emergency
sources.supports: When a toilet will not flush: use a working toilet elsewhere, or turn off the toilet's water valve, flush out the bowl, line it with a plastic kitchen garbage bag inside another, add an absorbent such as kitty litter, peat moss or lime, tie the inner bag when full, store used bags away from children, pets and wildlife, and wash hands with soap and running water (wipes and sanitizer if there is none); a five-gallon bucket with a seat works the same way; a 'cat hole' only if nothing else is possible and only for a day or two, on dry land at least 100 feet from wells, homes and open water, at least 6 inches deep and about 6 inches across, one use per hole; non-biodegradable items go in a bag in the garbage.
sources.notes: SOURCE DISAGREEMENT with health-osu-sanitation on disposal: this page says bagged waste can be put in the garbage can for disposal; the OSU Extension guide says human waste should not go in the normal garbage or landfill and should be stored until the public sanitary system is repaired. Our article tells readers to follow local authority instructions and flags the conflict. Read scope: full page as returned; linked county brochures not opened.

sources.title: Survival Basics: Sanitation and Waste Management (EM 9334)
sources.publisher: Oregon State University Extension Service (Kraemer, Hyde and Black)
sources.supports: Twin-bucket (separate urine and feces) emergency toilet: two 5-gallon buckets, heavy-duty 13-gallon bags of 3 to 5 mil for the feces bucket, about a half cup of carbon material (sawdust, wood shavings, shredded paper, bark chips or peat moss) after each use, fill the feces bucket no more than half full, double-bag and store waste away from food, water, pets and pests; dilute and pour urine on ground, changing location, and do not bury waste within 100 feet of a water source; do not put human waste in the normal garbage; handwashing station of a potable-water jug with spigot, soap, towels and a catch bucket, two stations if possible; hand sanitizer limits; turn off household water and avoid using toilets even if your own pipes seem fine, because street pipes may be broken; diapers, menstrual products and mobility considerations; supplies list.
sources.notes: Peer reviewed (Gray level per OSU). Written for the Pacific Northwest earthquake scenario but framed for any loss of water and sewer. Page metadata gives published 2021-10-14 and modified 2025-09-24; the visible date is October 2021. Read scope: full page as returned; the linked RDPO toilet guidebook, PHLUSH documents and the PDF edition were not opened.

sources.title: Be Prepared for a Power Outage (FEMA V-1008, December 2023)
sources.supports: One-page FEMA fact sheet: make a plan for refrigerating medicines and powering medical devices; talk to your doctor about how you will use electrically powered devices and store medications; 'Replace refrigerated medications if the power is out for a day or more, unless the drug's label says otherwise. Call your doctor or pharmacist if you depend on refrigerated medications that have been at room temperature. Only use the medicine until you have a new supply.'; generators outdoors at least 20 feet from building openings; learn the signs of carbon monoxide poisoning.
sources.notes: READ IN FULL: one page; text extracted with pdftotext from the saved PDF bytes (the first fetch tool could not decode it). Printed edition 'FEMA V-1008/December 2023'; exact day not printed, so 2023-12-01 is a placeholder for the month. File metadata shows last modified 2023-12-29. Wording says 'Replace', whereas the Ready.gov power-outage web page (updated 2026-06-04, health-ready-power-outages) says 'discard'; both are shown in medication-and-devices.
